SOURCE: "Agents' Last Exam" (ALE), Yiyou Sun, Xinyang Han, Weichen Zhang, Yuanbo Pang, Tianyu Wang, Yuhan Cao, Yixiao Huang, ... Dawn Song (plus a 15-person advisory committee and several hundred data contributors). Preprint; the only venue marking is "arXiv:2606.05405v4 [cs.AI] 25 Oct 2026". First author affiliation as printed: University of California, Berkeley ("Leading institution: University of California, Berkeley"). Funding: Tianqiao & Chrissy Chen Institute, Snorkel AI, UniPat AI.

COVERAGE: 40 of 40 pages, 141,087 of 141,087 chars, including appendices A-D. Skimmed: the contributor list (pp. 1, 16-18) and references (pp. 11-14). Figures 14-16 (pp. 38-40) are heatmaps; only the axis labels extract, not the cell values.

CLAIMS

- claim: The benchmark is 1,490 task instances across 55 subdomains in 13 domains, but only 150 are public and 323 are not yet through QC.
  number: 1,490 / 150 public / 1,017 private / 323 unverified
  setup: 960 external expert submissions plus 530 "commissioned ... internally authored"; Linux or Windows VMs
  quote: "The 1,490 task instances split into 960 external submissions (top, by first-pass review verdict) and 530 commissioned tasks (bottom). Each bar is segmented by release state: 150 public, 1,017 private, and 323 unverified pending QC."
  where: p5, Fig. 5

- claim: Tasks are past projects uploaded by practitioners and pass five gates: expert sourcing, submission, conference-style first-pass review, engineer implementation with dry-runs, and final committee QC of the reference output and tolerance bounds.
  number: none
  setup: all tasks; no rejection rate or reviewer agreement given
  quote: "verifies reference-output correctness, calibration of evaluation bounds (neither impossibly narrow nor spuriously permissive), and sufficiency of context"
  where: p5

- claim: Grading is an `evaluate()` function returning a score in [0,1] from output artifacts against a hidden `reference/` directory; 93.2% of task workflows are code-graded and 6.8% use an LLM judge.
  number: 93.2% / 6.8%; host-side 88.5%, VM-side 11.5%
  setup: static analysis of each `main.py` in the open-sourced task tree, at workflow level
  quote: "Code-based (deterministic) 93.2% LLM-as-judge 6.8%"
  where: p31, Table 4

- claim: The dominant scoring shape is gate-and-score: a binary precondition zeroes the task before any continuous metric counts.
  number: none (example weighting 0.70/0.30)
  setup: authors' static-analysis estimate, "the great majority" of evaluate() bodies
  quote: "failure on the gate forces the task score to 0 regardless of partial progress on other criteria"
  where: p7; example "score= 0.70·frac_within(0.3mm) + 0.30·frac_within(2.0mm)", p29

- claim: Where an LLM judge is used it answers narrow yes/no probes and code does the aggregation.
  number: none
  setup: creative/perceptual deliverables (renders, DAW sessions, animation)
  quote: "keep the LLM out of the role of integrator: the integration (weighting, gating, and aggregation across instances) always happens in code"
  where: p31

- claim: The best configuration fully passes about a quarter of the public tasks and none of the hardest tier, while mean partial-credit scores are far higher than pass rates.
  number: Codex + GPT-5.5: pass 38.1 / 22.7 / 0.0, score 64.7 / 36.0 / 11.2, overall pass 24.0
  setup: 67 Near-Term, 55 Full-Spectrum, 38 Last-Exam tasks; GUI-as-Tool; 5-hour cap per run
  quote: "Codex [33] (GPT-5.5 [35])38.164.7 ±2 $243 154h 550M 22.7 36.0 ±3 $157 125h 389M 0.0 11.2 ±2 $170 111h 754M24.0"
  where: p8, Table 1. Best Last-Exam pass by any configuration is 2.6% (one task of 38).

- claim: A run costs a few dollars and up to hours.
  number: $3-10 per run
  setup: frontier agents, average
  quote: "A single run of a frontier agent on one ALE task costs $3–10 on average and takes tens of minutes to hours."
  where: p9. Totals per configuration range from $87 (Cursor + Composer 2.5, 38.5% mean score) to $2,402 (Claude Code + Fable 5, 40.5%), p37.

- claim: Runs are repeated only for some configurations, and the spread is on mean score, not on pass rate.
  number: 3 runs
  setup: subset of Table 1 rows
  quote: "Superscript ± values denote score standard deviations estimated from three independent runs of the same task instance; due to compute budget constraints, only a subset of configurations include repeated runs."
  where: p8

- claim: Model choice moved the overall pass rate about three times as far as harness choice.
  number: 16.8 pp vs 4.9-7.2 pp
  setup: 12 models under OpenClaw; 5 harnesses on GPT-5.5; 3 on Opus 4.7
  quote: "Varying the backbone model under a fixed harness (OpenClaw, 12 models) produces a 16.8 pp spread, roughly 3× the spread observed when varying the harness under a fixed backbone (4.9–7.2 pp)."
  where: p36, Fig. 12

- claim: Failures were mostly wrong approach or missing domain knowledge, not execution.
  number: Approach 47% (wrong strategy 30%, abandoned 17%); Understanding 31% (domain knowledge 25%, fabrication 6%); Execution 22% (format 10%, bugs 8%, GUI 4%)
  setup: failed public-task runs of Claude Code + Opus 4.7 only; an LLM (Codex) wrote an analysis card per failure, GPT-4o at temperature 0 classified it; timeouts excluded
  quote: "Nearly half (47%) of classifiable failures stem from Approach errors: wrong strategy (30%) or premature abandonment (17%)."
  where: p36

- claim: Agents avoid the GUI even when the task is built around graphical software.
  number: 34%
  setup: public task instances
  quote: "34% of public task instances designate graphical software as the primary tool, yet the GUI share stays small across most configurations, as agents execute GUI tasks through Bash/CLI substitutes."
  where: p10

- claim: Timed-out runs are still scored on whatever is in the output directory.
  number: 3.8% of runs; mean score 20.7 vs 33.2
  setup: Table 1 runs, 5-hour cap
  quote: "3.8% of evaluated runs reached the cap. Runs that reached the cap have a mean score of 20.7, compared with 33.2 for runs that ended earlier."
  where: p34

- claim: The public subset tracks the full pool by domain.
  number: r=0.89
  setup: one configuration (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), 12 domain clusters; the full pool is easier
  quote: "(Pearson r=0.89, p<0.001)"
  where: p34

LIMITS
- No validation of any grader against people: no human-agreement figure for the code checks, the tolerances or the 6.8% LLM-judged workflows. QC is described, not measured.
- No human baseline, and no measured task duration; "Hours–Weeks" is asserted.
- The failure taxonomy is LLM-written and LLM-classified with no human check, on one configuration, with no failure count. GUI failure is defined under "Infrastructure" (p36) but counted under Execution in the distribution.
- No intervals on pass rates; the last tier rests on 38 tasks, so 2.6% is one task.
- No reward-hacking audit beyond design claims (hidden `reference/`, gates). No trajectory grading: only artifacts are scored.
- Per-task partial-credit weights are author choices with no sensitivity check.
- Internal inconsistencies: public set is 150 (p5), "152-task" (p9), and tiers sum to 160 with some tasks in two tiers; ALE-CLI is "105 tasks" but its tiers sum to 109; "250+" experts (abstract) vs "300+ practitioners" (p10); "draws every task from a real project" (p10) vs 530 internally authored; the intro says "under 10% on the hardest" where Table 1 shows 0.0% pass and 11.2 score; the abstract's "below 1%" refers to the hardest tier only.
- "Living benchmark" with rotating private tasks, so numbers will date. Only the 150 public tasks are reproducible.

BUILDS ON: SOC 2018 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2018) and O*NET (Peterson et al., 2001) for the taxonomy; GDPval (Patwardhan et al., 2025) and Remote Labor Index (Mazeika et al., 2025) as the human-graded predecessors; Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., ICLR 2026) and OSWorld (Xie et al., NeurIPS 2024) as the CLI-only and GUI-only subsets; ReAct (Yao et al., ICLR 2023) for the agent loop; OpenClaw for ALE-Claw.

CODE: none as code. Verbatim judge probes worth keeping (p30): "Does the candidate achieve a meaningful lowpoly reduction rather than effectively submitting the highpoly again?"; gate probe: "Does this screenshot provide evidence that the user has actually worked on the project ...".

FIGURES: Figure 6, p6, "Evaluation pipeline architecture". It shows `load()`/`start()`/`evaluate()` and the four-directory VM layout (`input/`, `software/`, `output/`, hidden `reference/`) in one picture, which is the environment-hygiene and state-grading contract faster than prose.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Table 1 extracts with fused cells ("38.164.7") and icon glyphs for cost and time; values are readable but check against the PDF before quoting. Heatmap values (Figs. 14-16) and Fig. 9 bar values did not extract. One Fig. 9(b) label reads "Codex (Opus)", which matches no Table 1 row.
